items.question: How do you experience the process of fundraising?
items.object: Fundraising and conversations with investors
items.answer: Nobody likes fundraising. It’s not that the outcome is hard; it’s just exhausting. You’re a broken record: you say the same thing over and over, and you get the same questions over and over. Really, I could record it and send it to all of you, right? Since your questions are all the same anyway. But amid this large amount of rather boring process, there are some conversations that are very exciting. Usually, those are with the investors you ultimately choose. For example, I remember very clearly a conversation I had with Howard Morgan from B Capital, our eventual lead investor.

items.question: What makes connections between different fields of mathematics especially beautiful to you?
items.object: Mathematical beauty in connections between fields
items.answer: When solving problems myself, that happens somewhat less frequently. But when I look at other people’s results, I often feel: wow, how can this be so beautiful? One example that particularly stands out is the first time I saw the modularity theorem for elliptic curves: every such modular form corresponds to an elliptic curve. It connects a comparatively algebraic expression with a more geometric object. I also remember other areas—probability and physics, for instance—where there are many results that I find very interesting.

items.question: What made learning quadratic reciprocity at the Ross Program a moment of being struck by mathematics for you?
items.object: Learning quadratic reciprocity at the Ross Program
items.answer: As for solving problems myself, when I was younger I perhaps had seen less, so I would think, mathematics can be played with like this too? At the Ross Program in the United States, starting from elementary number theory, we kept pushing all the way to quadratic reciprocity. Every day they gave you a problem set, and you had to finish all of it—there were quite a lot of problems—before you could get the next day’s set. It was like fighting monsters in a game. If you didn’t finish every problem, they wouldn’t give you the next set, and you would see that the student next to you was already three problem sets ahead of you, with more interesting and perhaps correct things. But because your proof ability had not caught up yet, you just could not get there. By the time we got to quadratic reciprocity, they presented many proofs. In that process, I definitely had moments of being struck by mathematics. You see that something expressed very concisely can have a very deep proof behind it, and can also have very creative solutions.

items.question: How do you understand what mathematics is?
items.object: Mathematics
items.answer: That really is not easy to answer. I think mathematics is a bit like this: humanity decides to create a system of civilization, and within that system, we build upward from certain axioms that we are willing to say—we consider to be true. To some extent, mathematicians have a contract: which things are we willing to accept as self-evident? And from those, we start with the fewest self-evident things—or not necessarily the fewest; it depends on the perspective. Some people look at it through compression: they want the fewest axioms. Some want to find the most interesting, or the most coherently assembled, system of axioms, and then build upward from there. In this process of building theories upward, many people think mathematics is problem-solving: I have a problem and I solve it. But the process of building theory upward is actually very interesting. Generally, you begin with mathematical examples—say, a sequence or a set—discover patterns, then feel what the next natural question should be, and prove it. So the process is a little like art. I think mathematics exists somewhere between art and science.

items.question: How do you understand the role of mathematical proof in getting unfamiliar discoveries accepted by other mathematicians?
items.object: Mathematical proof as a means of persuading mathematicians with different backgrounds
items.answer: I think that if mathematicians have fairly similar training backgrounds, or if they are in the same field and have read the same body of representative works, then to some extent they have a fairly strong shared understanding of what they believe should naturally be the case. Then, if something appears—for example, the most interesting case is when Ramanujan came from India to England and met Hardy and Littlewood. Hardy and Littlewood wrote papers together; they wrote many articles. Ramanujan arrived like an alien and said, “Hey, this is my notebook. Everything in it is true. I have never received mathematical training. I don’t know how to prove it.” Hardy and Littlewood would think these things looked interesting, new, and unlike what they had done before, yet still somehow felt right. So they began proving them. To some extent, proof allows a group of people unlike the original group of mathematicians to persuade them. Proof is, to some extent, influence: as long as I can prove something with airtight logic, my mathematical discovery can be accepted. And once it is accepted, of course, people then ask whether the proof is beautiful or not, natural or not. We saw many international number theorists look at Mr. Zhang Yitang’s number-theory proof and feel that its style was very different from the schools of thought familiar to them. But for that very famous result—the fixed gap between primes—they believed it was correct, so they accepted it. Then they began learning from and organizing one another’s proof methods. For example, James Maynard’s 2022 Fields Medal involved another set of proof techniques; his students inherited those techniques, and they and Mr. Zhang Yitang’s methods can be compared and simplified. This is an extremely interesting intellectual process.

items.question: How do you understand your own mathematical problem-solving style?
items.object: Her brute-force, symbolic approach to mathematical problem-solving
items.answer: I have always very much wanted to be an intuition-and-genius type. And this was a source of pain for me from a very young age, because I kept realizing that I did not have especially great mathematical talent. I am a brute-force type of player. When I was doing math Olympiads as a child, I remember people said the first problem on every paper—the Euclidean geometry problem—was guaranteed points. If you could not get the Euclidean geometry problem, you could not even win third prize. But I could never solve the Euclidean geometry problems. I might have been able to do algebraic inequalities. My brain may be more oriented toward algebraic symbolic expressions; geometry and topology were really poor. So I would represent every point and every line with complex numbers—brute force produces miracles. In the end, I did not need to understand the geometric meaning behind the problem; I would simply mechanically apply a very complicated complex-number method to solve it. I might need two or three times as long as others, which meant my time allocation for other problems could become uneven. But that was my only way of doing geometry. The most interesting thing is that starting in 2021, Google DeepMind began, very secretly, an AlphaGo-related project. They asked: if using AI to prove Euclidean geometry is very difficult, can we turn it into symbolic expressions? This was not the complex-number method I, a human, used, but the underlying philosophy was the same. I turn geometric figures into symbolic expressions. And then, using that, they were able to solve—I think—81 percent of historical IMO geometry problems.

items.question: How do you understand the value of your brute-force approach to mathematical research?
items.object: Her brute-force approach to mathematical research
items.answer: At MIT, everyone around me was naturally gifted. You only had to look left and right to know you were not. But I did not give up. I’m an indestructible cockroach. Give me a problem: if I cannot solve it in three months, I keep thinking. I remember Professor Henry Cohn gave me a small problem to think about concerning sphere packing in 28 dimensions. Of course, nobody expected an undergraduate to solve it completely. For six months I came up with nothing, but every week I would go and say, “Hey, this is what I tried. I did not succeed.” Then I tried another week and did not succeed again. But this brute-force type can, to some extent, complement naturally gifted players. There may be dirty and laborious work they do not want to do, and I can finish it.

items.question: How do you understand the roles of intuition and brute force in AI systems that solve mathematical problems?
items.object: Intuition and brute force in AI mathematics systems
items.answer:
I would say that within AI today, there are also relatively gifted, intelligent AIs and relatively brute-force AIs. For example, our company’s AI system is a system, so it contains many models. Some models can very quickly determine that a problem should probably be proved in one, two, three, four, five, six, or seven steps. Then there are AIs that lean toward formalization and have seen a great deal of formal languages like Lean. They say, “Anyway, I’ll just do one tactic after another.” A tactic is a step or strategy in Lean that lets you solve a very complex problem step by step. This type is more airtight: it takes small steps, rather than being the AI we just discussed that can outline a solution. So the two types of AI mathematicians within an AI system can complement each other.

In some cases, the most interesting thing is when they see a problem. We found recently that, in the Putnam Mathematical Competition for undergraduates, our company’s Axiom Prover AI received a perfect score. There have been five perfect scores in human history over the past 98 years. The first Putnam Competition began in 1927, and this was the sixth perfect score, achieved by an AI. We looked at the AI’s solutions. One problem particularly impressed me. A person on our team named Evan Chen, who coaches the U.S. IMO team and is an extremely gifted person, saw the problem and drew a diagram. The moment everyone in the conference room saw that diagram, we said, “Oh, then you’ve solved it”—a solution based on one diagram.

items.question: Why do you hesitate to call progress in automated theorem proving an AI victory?
items.object: AI-assisted automated theorem proving
items.answer: This field cannot really be called an AI victory. Before AI and deep neural networks, there was already a group of computer scientists who hoped to enable rule-based computer systems to help humans solve solvable mathematical problems. That is called automated theorem proving, ATP. Then ITP means interactive theorem proving: there were always things ATP could not solve, so in the past mathematicians would write in specialized programming languages like Lean and work with computer systems to prove things. Now we have merely replaced the human in ITP with an AI. I see this old discipline as, to some extent, an intersection of ATP and AI.

items.question: Why do you consider free attention important for entrepreneurs and mathematicians?
items.object: Free attention in entrepreneurship and mathematics
items.answer: Free attention means unconstrained attention. For example, every morning we wake up and see many emails, and there are many things we must execute. If we do not execute them, perhaps there is a deadline and we must get them done. At that point, the brain is in a state of constrained attention—that kind of state. Many very successful entrepreneurs are highly disciplined executors. Day after day, they compound the returns on their execution. That is good. So when I first started a company, I also very much wanted to do a certain number of things every day. But free attention is actually what distinguishes an average entrepreneur from a very good entrepreneur with strategy and judgment. It is in free attention—or, for a mathematician, in free attention—that the gap between people can widen. If you voluntarily fill all your time by saying, “I want to work like military training; every day I have to get a certain amount of work done,” you may end up neglecting your free attention and losing many opportunity costs. So I especially miss walking to school as a child, when there was a lot of free attention. To some extent, it is like what people call Einstein’s shower time. In that process, the mind can go to many very interesting places.

items.question: How do you understand your own entrepreneurial style in relation to visionaries, executors, and salespeople?
items.object: Entrepreneurial styles and her own optimistic approach
items.answer: People say there are three kinds of entrepreneurs. The first is the visionary, an ambitious person with foresight. The second is execution—the executor. Zuckerberg, for example, is an execution maniac. He is someone who executes, executes, executes, executes, executes. You can see that at intervals he takes action to make up for possibly lagging visionary decisions. So he is a very execution-oriented entrepreneur. The third is the salesperson. Sales is not a negative word: this person has excellent communication skills, a strong ability to communicate with different audiences, can influence and lead people, and can build a team. I have never thought I was a salesperson; I definitely am not. And I am not such a good executor either. Perhaps I cannot be called visionary, either—not in the sense that my foresight is necessarily correct. I just want to do certain things, and I become extremely optimistic about them. When I am extremely optimistic, even if things fall somewhat short, it still seems okay; a KPI has still been achieved.

It is collaborative, and collaboration needs a good structure and a way to split a task into small tasks. I think this process is very interesting. items.question: What kind of mathematical work would you most want AI to help you with?
items.object: AI assistance with mathematical proofs
items.answer:
What I saw at the time was: everything we regard as impossible may be possible. And if that is so, what would mean most to me personally is AI helping me do mathematical proofs—especially because I am not a naturally gifted player. To some extent, who can AI help the most? Brute-force mathematicians—people like me. I may truly have to enumerate countless possibilities and spend many days verifying a very standard argument, a standard proof method, comparing things against it.

I remember a paper by Professor Ben Green called “Sárközy theorem for shifted primes.” It says: I have a set, and I want to ensure that the difference between two elements A and B in it, A minus B, is not p plus 1 or p minus 1, where p is prime; how large can such a set be among the numbers from 1 to n? When I read it, I thought: how many mathematical problems can this be used to prove? The same machinery—Professor Ben Green's inventions or discoveries—can be applied to function fields; you can apply it to shifted sums of two squares. Maybe there is no great significance in doing that; you can do x squared plus y squared plus or minus 1. I do not know whether that has great significance, but this whole toolkit can be used for many things.

AI should solve it completely. AI should reach the level of a PhD student who is highly proficient with every number-theory tool and technique in Davenport. I thought this had to be possible, and I began thinking about how to do it: you need compute.

items.question: How do you view DeepMind’s 2024 AlphaProof result in the development of AI for mathematics?

items.question: How do you understand the connection between mathematics, programming, and real-world testing in your AGI worldview?

Why is code math? Because we now find that backend work, even entire distributed-system web coding, cannot be done as well as building a website precisely because there are many things where it cannot backtrack and cannot decompose hierarchically well. So our AGI worldview is mathematics, then programming, then real-world testing, then everything else.

items.question: How do you think language models and formal-verification tools should work together in an AI-for-Math system?
items.object: AI for Math as a system combining language models and formal verification
items.answer: I think it is a very good setup: you can try things on it that you think will succeed. This may be hard to do in other domains that are not as clean, but here I think we can do it. For example, I think AI for Math roughly has a paradigm, right? Starting with “Draft, Sketch and Proof,” a 2022 paper: first, have the informal model make an outline; second, turn that outline formal, into Lean; then fill in all the intermediate `sorry`s. Sorry—sorry is a tactic, a piece of syntax in Lean. It means, “I will not prove this part, but you know it must be true”; it is like asking you to take it for granted. Step one is draft: outline, informal. Step two is sketch: formalize the outline. Step three is proof: fill in every `sorry`. There are several ways to fill them: AI; something with a neural network; or the old ATP-style, purely rule-based approach without AI, to fill them automatically—for example, a hammer. Lean has something called a hammer. A hammer is, as the name suggests, an axe: one swing and the `sorry` is gone. The history of Lean hammers is especially interesting. Long ago other languages had them, such as Isabelle, another theorem-proving language, and Coq, later renamed Rocq. They had hammers—for example, I think “Match the Hammer” was an Isabelle hammer. Lean had no hammer until, I recall, last June, when several people at CMU released a Lean hammer. But it was not sufficient; its functionality did not cover all the capabilities attempted by other hammers. At the time we told Leo de Moura, Lean’s founder, that Axiom hoped to sponsor a fully open-source Lean hammer for the whole community. Later, perhaps they simply did not have enough people—not funding—so it did not happen. But this year something new came out called Grind, G-R-I-N-D. To some extent, Grind can solve many mathematical problems. I have seen demos from other AI-for-Math companies where, if you just run Grind, it can solve the problem directly, with no AI involved. We see the world as AI and formal verification—two forces—working together on a problem. Wherever a deterministic rather than probabilistic system can solve it, we use that; we also use whatever abstractions Lean itself can make, solving as much as possible. It is a good system setup: first use the simplest, cheapest thing; if it can solve it, solve it. Then use the larger language-model systems for what remains.

items.question: Why do you see sub-agents as a promising way to scale AI for Math?

In a math problem, an experience is a data trail: a segment of the whole process that leads to ultimately solving the problem. All of that can serve as experience. As you let sub-agents use skills—and skills are learning to use tools—then, as the variety of choices grows, you can scale learning from experience. That is the first point where I think we may be doing well.

items.question: What do you find beautiful about bringing code generation and proof generation together?
items.object: The transfer from mathematical theorem proving to code verification and generation
items.answer: The second aha moment was discovering that a very good AI theorem prover for mathematics can translate into very strong code-verification capability. On the Verina benchmark, we saw a result that surprised all of us, and it can generate code and proofs at the same time. That is very interesting. Ordinary code is Python and the proof is English, natural language. If you do reinforcement learning, it is as if it points you in two directions: should you become good at Python or at natural language? But if you bring the two objective functions together, so both the code and its proof are Lean—or even if the code is not Lean but Rust: Lean is dependent type theory, and Rust is a strongly typed language—this convergence may enable better verify-generation, generating while verifying. That is the second thing I personally find beautiful.

items.question: How do you understand the approach that AI for Math has converged on?
items.object: The prevailing approach to AI for Math
items.answer: I think AI for Math has now converged on roughly one approach. First take an open-source pretrained model—say, Qwen—and do post-training on it. People differ in how they do that: some go straight to RL; some do SFT and then RL. After making the model, put it into a system. The system has various models, some of which do very specialized things, and it calls tools. Some tools are quite difficult to build; they require a great deal of Lean metaprogramming. There are different ways to design the whole system, but this is roughly what everyone is doing now. There are still minor differences. I think our approach is relatively similar to C Prover and Hypert Prover.

items.question: How do you understand the broader potential of AI for Math beyond solving math problems?
items.object: The broader uses of AI for Math and the relationship between proving and conjecturing
items.answer: I think this is a very interesting point. When people talk about AI for Math, they generally talk about one core technology: proving. But what AI for Math can do—what has broader uses—is really a whole set of things. You need a very good prover, a proof system; you need a very good conjecturer, an AI that can pose conjectures and mathematical problems. To some extent, the proving AI is the reward for the conjecturing AI: I can use the prover as the reward signal for conjectures.

items.question: How do you assess the Self-play Theorem Prover paper’s approach to evaluating mathematical conjectures?
items.object: The Self-play Theorem Prover (STP) paper and its approach to evaluating conjectures
items.answer: That paper was by Dong Kefan and Ma Tengyu at Stanford. It was the starting point for everyone’s thinking about models for conjecturing. The challenge with a conjecture model is that, unlike a proving model, where proving it is one and failing is zero, I do not have a reward for whether a conjecture is good. Besides using something provable as grounding, as a signal, you need other things—for example, how do you know whether a conjecture is mathematically meaningless? Perhaps you have conjectured something completely unimportant; I do not know why you would ask your prover to prove it. There may be something called an elegance filter, to judge whether it is elegant. In the STP paper, elegance is determined by length: whether the statement is longer or shorter than its proof. But that feels very crude. Their dataset, Lean Workbook, is more or less a high-school-math dataset. At more advanced levels, undergraduate or doctoral research, you cannot rely on length as the sole filter for elegance. It does not extend particularly well as difficulty rises; the paper is insufficient.

items.question: Why do you consider a knowledge base such an important component of AI for formal mathematical proof?
items.object: Knowledge bases and autoformalization for formal mathematical proof
items.answer: Another very important component, especially when doing formal mathematical proof, is the knowledge base. It matters because most existing mathematics—in English or Chinese—does not exist in Lean; even the definitions are not in Lean. I need two things: first, the ability to search well for what is known and proved, and what needs proving. Or, if you ask me to prove something and I find a counterexample among the known results, I can falsify it immediately, right? Second, I need to convert this vast body of mathematics into formal data. That conversion is the second core technology I mentioned: autoformalization. It is not proving; it is conversion.

items.question: Why do you think converting existing mathematics into formal Lean code is an overlooked challenge in AI for mathematics?
items.object: Autoformalization of existing mathematics into Lean
items.answer: This conversion is, to some extent, overlooked. If you prove many Putnam or IMO problems, you can go on Twitter and say, “Hey, I proved them; I am a great AI mathematician.” But if you merely convert mathematics humans have already discovered and written into formal form, you get less praise. Yet this technology is as hard as proving, at least; I think it is harder. Why? If I set a strict requirement—input is a mathematical article on arXiv, output is Lean code for every theorem-and-proof pair in that article—then there are several steps. items.question: How do you think about conversion between natural-language mathematics and Lean within your vision for AI for Math?
items.object: Conversion between natural-language mathematics and Lean
items.answer: It requires strong decomposition, decomposition-reasoning ability. So on the island of AI for Math as I see it, there is a prover, a conjecturer, a knowledge base, and conversion ability running through all of them. That is our technological vision. You might ask: isn’t this just translation, translating English into Lean? In fact it is not. English and French are similarly abstract; their degrees of structure or lack of structure, looseness and rigor are quite similar. But Lean is a computer-code language, more like Python. The conversion is especially difficult because AI has seen very little Lean; all Lean in the world adds up to not many tokens. The reverse conversion is autoinformalization, Lean back to English. That is easier because it has seen much more English. But the difficulty is how to ensure that the mathematics translated back is completely correct. Usually we convert it into Lean again—convert it there, convert back, then convert it there again and see whether it matches. This is called cycle consistency.

items.question: How do you see the value of turning mathematics into code for AI?
items.object: Turning mathematics into code for AI
items.answer: For example, algebraic geometry has the word germ, G-E-R-M. In English, germ means a bacterium. I was studying algebraic geometry during the pandemic, which made the germ jokes especially amusing: its probability distribution there is certainly different from its distribution in English. So if you want AI to do mathematics in English, that is not very good—or at least absolutely not the whole picture. If you turn mathematics into code, then because of the verifiability we discussed, I think it makes much more sense. For example, Lean programs are written quite logically and handle some logical reasoning fairly well. Lean, as an automated formal-proof language, has siblings: Coq, Rocq, Isabelle, and older SMT and SAT systems, right? These are logic-based proof languages. Almost all chip verification in the world now uses Jasper from Cadence, which is SMT-based. Jasper has many limitations. An interesting question—or brainstorm—is: what would the world look like if all the struggling SMTs in the world could be replaced by Lean?

items.question: How do you think about your responsibility as a company leader when people and work come into conflict?

items.answer: They have conflicted before. We have also let interns go; we have had conflicts. At the same time, I have another side: often, why do you need to think for a long time? Often, when you feel people and work are in conflict, it is actually because you yourself are not good enough.
